justice: The paved carriageway is wide and newly marked, but space allocation heavily favors motor traffic while no formal sidewalk is visible on either side.
The road edges transition into dirt shoulders and construction debris piles, indicating that non-motorized users receive lower-quality space than drivers.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or barrier-free pedestrian facilities are visible, limiting accessibility for a broad range of users.
Streetlights are provided along the corridor, which distributes some public infrastructure evenly, but supporting facilities for walkers and cyclists are largely absent.
safety: The road has clear centerline and edge line markings, which helps lane guidance for drivers.
There is no separated sidewalk or protected cycling lane, so pedestrians and cyclists would need to use the roadway edge or dirt shoulder.
Loose soil, rock piles, and uneven shoulders on the right side create roadside hazards and reduce recovery space for all users.
Long sightlines and sparse traffic improve visibility, but the wide, straight alignment may also encourage higher vehicle speeds.
livability: The corridor appears isolated, with vacant vegetated lots and very limited active frontage directly along the street.
No benches, bus stops, shops, or community amenities are visible at street level, reducing day-to-day usefulness for public life.
The distant residential towers are set back and do not create an active or engaging street edge here.
The environment feels transitional or under development rather than a completed neighborhood street that supports social interaction.
sustainability: The abundant roadside vegetation provides some ecological value compared with a fully sealed corridor.
Streetlights and fresh paving suggest investment in infrastructure, but there is no visible support for public transport, walking, or protected cycling.
Wide asphalt coverage prioritizes motorized travel and increases heat-absorbing surface area.
Unpaved shoulders, exposed soil, and construction rubble suggest incomplete stormwater-sensitive design and weak green-street integration.
aesthetics: The streetlights are evenly spaced and the new asphalt surface gives the corridor a relatively orderly appearance.
Open sky and green roadside vegetation create a spacious visual scene.
Construction debris piles, bare dirt shoulders, and unfinished edges reduce visual quality.
Utility poles and transmission infrastructure on the left add an industrial character that weakens scenic appeal.
comfort: There is almost no tree canopy or built shade over the walking zone, so thermal comfort would be poor in hot sunny weather.
No seating, shelters, or pedestrian rest areas are visible along the corridor.
The road surface for vehicles appears smooth, but the pedestrian realm consists largely of dirt shoulders and uneven edges, reducing physical comfort off the carriageway.
Low traffic volume and broad open space may reduce crowding stress, yet the isolated setting can feel psychologically uncomfortable for some users.
walkability: No dedicated sidewalk is visible, forcing pedestrians onto the road edge or rough dirt shoulder.
There are no marked crosswalks, curb ramps, refuge islands, or pedestrian signals visible in the scene.
The corridor is straight and legible, but its scale and lack of frontage activity make walking less attractive.
Minimal shade and no street-level amenities such as benches or shelters further weaken walkability.
bikeability: The roadway is relatively wide and smooth, which gives cyclists some operating space in low-traffic conditions.
However, there is no protected bike lane, painted cycle track, or bicycle-specific signage.
Dirt shoulders, debris piles, and unfinished roadside edges reduce safe maneuvering space for cyclists.
The long straight corridor may support direct travel, but speed differentials with motor vehicles could make cycling uncomfortable.
